title: Finish, price, submit and learn from every proposal
course_title: Proposal Writing: Grants and Business Proposals

say: Finish, price, submit, and learn from every proposal.
This is the video for module four of Proposal Writing.
The executive summary is the most read part of any proposal. Some reviewers decide from it alone. It must make sense on its own, so write it last.

say: The cover letter introduces your proposal on your letterhead, signed by your leader. One page: the right name and call, the project, amount and duration, why it fits, what is enclosed, and your contacts.
Then do the consistency check. List your key facts and search the document for each one. If the cover letter says 4,815,000 but the budget shows 4,850,000, reviewers start to doubt everything.

A client does not care about your theory of change. She wants to know exactly what she will get, when, and for how much. The biggest danger is unclear scope, which leads to disputes and unpaid extra work.

panel.heading: Vague scope or protective scope?
left: Supply liquid soap to the school

say: Amaka's school proposal starts with the bursar's own need, then lists what is included: 60 litres a month in sealed 5-litre jerrycans, labelled, delivered on the first Monday of each month.
It also lists what is not included, such as dispensers. Exclusions feel awkward, but they protect both sides.

panel.heading: Vague scope or protective scope?
left: Supply liquid soap to the school

say: A deposit of 50%, 45,000 naira, is paid on acceptance, because she must buy materials first. The price is valid for 30 days.

Ask clients to pay only into your business account, and confirm every transfer in your banking app, never from a screenshot. If the school later asks for dispensers, they are quoted separately and agreed in writing first.

say: Save the confirmation or sent email. For a grant, wait for the funder's timeline. For a client, follow up within a few days, offer a short call, and mention the price validity date.

panel.rule: Follow up politely. Never try to influence reviewers.

say: Keep a simple tracker of every proposal: date, funder or client, amount, status, feedback and lessons. Your win rate is proposals won, divided by proposals decided, times 100.

cards.d: 6 sent: 1 won, 4 lost, 1 waiting. 1 won divided by 5 decided.
10 sent: 6 accepted, 3 declined, 1 no response. 6 divided by 9 decided.
Always write budget notes. Check priorities before writing. Offer a smaller monthly volume.

say: Your practice. Assemble your full proposal with an executive summary and cover letter, and check every key fact matches. Write a client proposal with inclusions, exclusions, price and an acceptance page.
Then set up your tracker and a polite follow-up template. Now continue with the lessons below.
